{"piece_id":"02","markdown":"# The Check Is the Capability

## Scene 1 — The answer

**Narration:** Which CAD-agent claims withstand scrutiny? The answer is: claims hold only as far as the check that observed them. CAD agents now merit attention as first-draft and workflow tools. But producing geometry, or running a workflow, does not prove engineering readiness. As of October 16, 2026, the practical question is narrower: what property was checked, by whom, and does that check match the downstream decision? This video uses AI-generated presentation.

**Visual:** Title card. On-screen rule: “Claim → observed check → supported conclusion.” Under it: “Generated CAD ≠ generally engineering-ready.”

**Source on screen:** Agentic 3D, “The Check Is the Capability,” October 16, 2026. Sources cited throughout.

## Scene 2 — What the broader record says

**Narration:** First, a reported fact from the MIT Computational Design and Fabrication Group survey. It says frontier models build parametric parts and assemblies. That means editable CAD output is now a meaningful capability. But the same survey says tolerance specifications and manufacturability have not been tested on physical parts. So an editable model is not proof that it conforms to drawing tolerances or production constraints.

**Visual:** Split diagram. Left: “Checked: parametric parts and assemblies.” Right: “Not established: tolerance conformance; manufacturability on physical parts.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c1 — MIT Computational Design and Fabrication Group, “On the Opportunities and Risks of Frontier Models for 3D Modeling, Computational Design and Robotics,” September 22, 2026.

## Scene 3 — A concrete Backflip check

**Narration:** Engineering.com provides a small, concrete example. Its reviewer imported a Backflip STEP output into Fusion, applied material, and checked mass. For the first drawing-to-CAD task, Engineering.com reports that Backflip got the mass exactly correct. The article also reports a second selected drawing that passed the mass comparison.

This is a reported result from Engineering.com. The observed check was mass agreement after material assignment in Fusion.

**Visual:** Flow: “Backflip STEP output → Fusion → apply material → check mass.” Green result badge: “First task: exactly correct.” Small label: “Selected drawings; not production shop drawings.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c2, 02-c3 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026.

## Scene 4 — What that result does and does not show

**Narration:** Here is the core test applied. A mass check supports mass agreement for that test. It does not support tolerance conformance or manufacturability. That is an interpretation based on the scope of the check and the MIT survey’s stated gap.

For a workflow that needs a mass estimate on that particular output, this check is useful. But it did not inspect every feature, dimensions at tolerance, or whether a shop can make the part.

**Visual:** A labeled boundary. Inside: “Observed: mass agreement.” Outside, crossed or unverified: “Feature-level correctness,” “Tolerance conformance,” “Manufacturability.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c6 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026; MIT Computational Design and Fabrication Group, “On the Opportunities and Risks of Frontier Models for 3D Modeling, Computational Design and Robotics,” September 22, 2026.

## Scene 5 — Counterexamples in the same test

**Narration:** The same Engineering.com test shows why broad claims break down. Engineering.com reports that, on a multibody drawing-to-CAD task, Backflip created only one of seven bodies. It also reports that Backflip’s Fusion add-in only partially recreated geometry for one tested part.

These results do not negate the selected mass checks. They separate distinct capabilities: producing a solid, handling multibody models, preserving geometry through an integration, and reconstructing editable native features.

**Visual:** Capability matrix. Rows: “Mass agreement,” “Multibody handling,” “Fusion reconstruction.” Results: “Passed selected checks,” “1 of 7 bodies,” “Partial geometry.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c4, 02-c5 — Engineering.com, “Welcome to the vibe-CAD era,” September 30, 2026.

## Scene 6 — Commercial workflow claims

**Narration:** Commercial workflow announcements should receive the same treatment. SimScale says its Engineering AI Agent can propose a setup, mesh a CAD model, run physics, and report results in Onshape. Onshape says its FeatureScript MCP Server lets LLMs help create, test, debug, and refine custom CAD functionality.

Those are source claims about offered workflows, not independent measurements of correctness. Teams should verify the setup, mesh, boundary conditions, code, and outputs against the decision each artifact will support.

**Visual:** Two workflow cards, each labeled “Source claim.” SimScale card: setup, mesh, physics, report. Onshape card: create, test, debug, refine. Footer: “Check the resulting engineering artifacts.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c7 — Engineering.com, “Multiphysics gets MCP server and Onshape gets SimScale agent,” September 23, 2026. 02-c8 — Onshape, “5 Ways Teams Can Leverage the Onshape FeatureScript MCP Server,” September 30, 2026.

## Scene 7 — Simulation-ready is also bounded

**Narration:** NVIDIA describes a more explicit staged check set for CAD-to-simulation assets. NVIDIA says its workflow checks imported robot scale, parts, and appearance against references. It says the workflow configures joints, collision geometry, and physical properties for arms and grippers. Then it runs selected sim-ready foundation checks and a grasp test, fixes issues, and reruns them.

These source claims support visual consistency, configured simulation properties, and simulated grasp behavior. They do not report physical-transfer outcomes or prove real-world robot reliability.

**Visual:** Three-step pipeline: “Reference comparison,” “Physics configuration,” “Foundation checks + grasp test → fix → rerun.” Boundary label: “Validated in simulation, not reported physical transfer.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c9 — NVIDIA, “5 Steps to Create SimReady Assets for Robotics with Frontier AI Models,” October 8, 2026, 00:20–00:28. 02-c10 — NVIDIA, 00:28–00:37. 02-c11 — NVIDIA, 00:37–00:47.

## Scene 8 — What to do next

**Narration:** One supporting example points to a better evaluation design. The Physical AI Podcast reports that, in a Black Forest Labs-commissioned evaluation, the operator was blind to which model was driving. The claimant also commissioned the evaluation, and the transcript-derived numerical details were not independently audio-verified here. Treat this as a design feature to seek, not proof that a system is ready.

For product leaders, start procurement with the downstream decision, not the demo. Require a representative test that observes the specific property you need: bodies, feature history, mating relationships, tolerances, simulation setup, or manufacturability. Watch next for disclosed, reproducible evaluations on tolerance-critical drawings, multibody and assembly tasks, native editability, and manufactured or physically tested outputs.

**Visual:** Procurement checklist: “Name the decision,” “Name the property,” “Run a representative check,” “Record what remains unverified.” End card: “The check is the capability.”

**Source on screen:** 02-c12 — Physical AI Podcast, “Black Forest Labs Beat NVIDIA, Figure's Rival Did the Maths,” September 26, 2026, 04:26–04:32.
